prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "WELLS FARGO & COMPANY/MN" (ticker WFC), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "WFC", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: Wells Fargo & Company
result.industry: Diversified US banking and financial services
markets: Mortgages, auto loans and credit cards
Corporate and investment banking, commercial real estate lending and markets
Wealth and investment management (Wells Fargo Advisors, private bank)

mission.plain: Wells Fargo says it aims to meet its customers' financial needs and help them succeed financially.

about.plain: Wells Fargo is one of the biggest banks in the United States. People keep their money in its checking and savings accounts, and it lends money for homes, cars and credit cards. It also helps businesses borrow, move money and raise funds, and helps families invest. It earns money mostly from the gap between interest it charges on loans and pays on deposits, plus fees.
about.customers: Tens of millions of American households, small businesses, mid-sized and large companies, and wealthy investors buy its services.
about.everyday: The red-and-yellow stagecoach logo is on thousands of bank branches and ATMs across the US, and many people pay with a Wells Fargo debit or credit card.

money.plain: checking, savings, mortgages, cards, car loans
loans, deal advice and trading for big companies
loans and payment services for mid-sized firms

money.part: Balance-sheet growth after the asset cap was lifted (June 2025)
money.plain: growing loans, deposits and trading again

result.summary: Wells Fargo has a real but moderate moat built on scale, cheap and sticky deposits and switching costs in everyday banking. Its brand and control processes were badly damaged by the 2016 sales-practices scandal, and the Federal Reserve's asset cap held its balance sheet flat from 2018 until June 2025; returns (16.3% ROTCE in Q3 2026) are improving but still trail JPMorgan.

pricingPower.evidence: Like other large banks it pays depositors well below market rates on much of its $1.5 trillion deposit base, yet deposits still grew from $1,367.4B (Sep 2025) to $1,502.7B (Sep 2026); however its net interest margin fell to 2.43% in Q3 2026 from 2.61% a year earlier, showing loan and deposit pricing follows rates and competition.

moats.evidence: Wells Fargo is one of the four largest US banks with a 170-year-old stagecoach brand, but the 2016 fake-accounts scandal damaged trust and the brand is no longer a clear advantage over Chase or Bank of America.

Checking accounts with direct deposit, autopay, mortgages and business treasury services are tedious to move, so deposits are sticky: total deposits reached $1,502.7B at September 30, 2026, up from $1,367.4B a year earlier.
Banking has limited network effects; Wells Fargo benefits modestly from Zelle (which it co-owns with other big banks) and its large ATM and branch network, but these are shared or easily matched.

With about $2.25 trillion of assets and roughly $1.5 trillion of deposits, Wells Fargo funds itself cheaply and spreads technology and compliance costs over a huge base; its efficiency ratio improved to 63% in Q3 2026 from 65% a year earlier.
Only a handful of US banks have the national branch footprint, capital and regulatory standing to serve consumers, middle-market companies and large corporates at Wells Fargo's scale.
Wells Fargo is an incumbent being challenged by digital banks and fintechs rather than a disruptor of others.
Its risk and control processes were found deficient for years (the Fed's asset cap was only lifted in June 2025), so process quality is a catching-up story rather than an edge.
Its main scarce asset is a national bank charter with one of the largest US deposit bases and branch networks, which is valuable but shared with a few peers.

customers.evidence: Wells Fargo scored 79 in the ACSI 2026 finance study (up 1%), level with the national-bank average and Bank of America and below JPMorgan Chase's 80; trust is still recovering from the 2016 fake-accounts scandal.

talent.evidence: It is a large, well-known employer but has been shrinking headcount (205,198 at end-2025 versus 217,502 a year earlier, with Q3 2026 headcount down another 8%), and it is not usually ranked among the top banks to work for, behind JPMorgan and Goldman Sachs.

product.evidence: Its products are solid and broad (Autograph and Active Cash cards, mobile app, Wells Fargo Advisors) but rarely best in class; JPMorgan Chase leads on customer satisfaction (ACSI 80 vs 79) and investment-banking rankings.

marketShare.measure: share of US deposits (Wells Fargo is among the top 3 US deposit holders with $1,502.7B at Sep 30, 2026; exact shares not verified)

threats: Falling interest rates and deposit competition squeezing net interest margin (2.43% in Q3 2026 vs 2.61% a year earlier)
Lingering regulatory and reputational risk from the 2016 sales-practices scandal; any new enforcement action could again restrict growth
Thinner capital buffer after running CET1 down to 10.0% (from 11.0%) to fund buybacks and loan growth
Credit losses in commercial real estate and consumer lending in a downturn (provision rose to $1,029M in Q3 2026 from $681M)
Digital banks, fintechs and private-credit funds taking deposits, payments and corporate lending
Larger rivals JPMorgan and Bank of America outspending it on technology and AI

ceo.name: Charles W. Scharf
ceo.background: Johns Hopkins BA, NYU Stern MBA; former CEO of Visa (2012-2016) and BNY Mellon (2017-2019); Wells Fargo chairman since 2025

c1.evidence: Wells Fargo is a 174-year-old incumbent in mature US banking, where FY2025 revenue of $83.7B was only 4% a year above FY2022's $74.4B.

c2.evidence: Customers mostly choose it for convenience (thousands of branches and ATMs) and sticky existing relationships rather than a unique product, an advantage shared by JPMorgan Chase and Bank of America.

c3.evidence: Almost every American knows the stagecoach brand, but it is not the default leader (JPMorgan Chase is), and its ACSI 2026 score of 79 only matches the national-bank average.

c4.evidence: Wells Fargo does not prominently promote a distinctive mission; management's emphasis since 2019 has been fixing risk controls, cutting costs and raising returns (ROTCE 16.3% in Q3 2026).

c6.evidence: “big, scandal-hit, recovering”: the public strongly associates the name with the 2016 fake-accounts scandal, so the impression is mixed, though improving after regulators lifted the asset cap in June 2025.

c7.evidence: US banking is a very large market but grows roughly with the economy; there is no strong secular tailwind beyond wealth management and payments digitisation.

c8.evidence: With the asset cap gone it can again grow its balance sheet, investment bank and markets business (CIB revenue $19.2B in FY2025), but it remains a US-focused bank without a large new market.

m1.evidence: Charlie Scharf is a disciplined operator focused on controls, efficiency and returns rather than a visionary with a new picture of finance.

m2.evidence: Scharf is a hired professional manager (CEO since October 2019) but has taken a long-term approach to a multi-year regulatory clean-up.

m4.evidence: He has rebuilt controls and customer remediation, but has also cut headcount sharply (205,198 at end-2025 vs 217,502 a year earlier), so servant leadership is not his defining trait.

m5.evidence: His cultural changes centred on risk management and accountability, not on a culture of product invention.

m6.evidence: Scharf has deep payments and banking-operations experience (ex-CEO of Visa) but no engineering background.

m7.evidence: There is no clear public evidence either way that his stewardship is aimed beyond running a sound, profitable bank.

m7b.evidence: No commencement speech by Charlie Scharf at a top university was found.

m8b.evidence: Scharf is a low-profile, reserved banker without a widely known public persona.

m9.evidence: Under Scharf, Wells Fargo exited most consent orders, had the Fed asset cap lifted in June 2025, and lifted ROTCE from 9.3% in 2022 to 14.6% in 2025 and 16.3% in Q3 2026.

m10.evidence: He has run a long cost-cutting programme, with headcount down every year and the efficiency ratio at 63% in Q3 2026, though it is still higher than at JPMorgan.

c10.evidence: It serves tens of millions of US households and businesses with essential payments, savings and credit, but its impact is mostly domestic and not life-changing.

p2.evidence: Running a $2.25 trillion regulated bank safely is hard and important to the US economy, but the services themselves are widely offered by peers.

f2.evidence: Pre-tax margin rose from 3% in 2020 to 30% in 2025 (income before tax $25.2B on $83.7B revenue), but it fell from 37% in 2021; banks report no gross margin.

f3.evidence: Shareholders' equity is positive at $177.9B (Sep 2026) and CET1 is 10.0%, but like all banks it is highly leveraged, with $221.0B of borrowings and $1.5 trillion of deposits.

f4.evidence: Income before tax rose from $2.5B in 2020 to $25.2B in 2025 but dipped to $15.6B in 2022; bank operating cash flow is volatile and not meaningful.

v1.evidence: Its checking, cards and advice are comparable to JPMorgan Chase and Bank of America, with no clear practical reason to pick it over them.

v2.evidence: Wells Fargo is not typically cited among the best places to work in finance; it has been cutting staff (headcount down 8% year on year in Q3 2026).

c5.evidence: Millions of customers and businesses would be disrupted if it vanished, but rivals could absorb its deposits and loans, so the loss would be inconvenient rather than irreplaceable.
